analysis.one_liner: Requires federal licenses and dealer-recorded sales for handguns and detachable-magazine semiautomatic rifles.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required anyone owning a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that takes a detachable magazine to hold a federal firearm owner license, obtainable only after fingerprints, a background check, and an application through a licensed dealer. Every future sale or transfer of those guns would have to go through a licensed dealer who verifies the buyer's license and reports the transaction to the Attorney General, creating a federal record of sale. It also adds new crimes: failing to report a lost or stolen gun, leaving a loaded gun where a child can reach it, and possessing a covered gun without a license, punishable by up to 10 years in prison.
analysis.who_benefits: People living with gun violence, especially in communities the bill's findings say are hit hardest — the bill cites FBI data that about 73-77 percent of criminal homicides in 2019-2020 were firearms-related, and that Black and Latino children face elevated gun-death risk. Law enforcement would gain a record of sale system to trace guns used in crime.

how_it_helps.text: Requires a fingerprint-based background check and a license before a person can possess a handgun or a semiautomatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine larger than 10 rounds.

Routes every private sale or transfer of a covered gun through a licensed dealer, who must verify the buyer's license and report the sale — including serial number, model, and both parties' information — to the Attorney General within 14 days.
Makes it a federal crime to fail to report a lost or stolen covered firearm within 72 hours, closing a channel through which guns reach the illegal market.

Creates a child access prevention offense, punishable by up to 5 years, for leaving a loaded firearm accessible to a child who then causes death or serious injury, with exceptions for securely stored guns and lawful self-defense.
Directs the Attorney General to build a firearm injury information clearinghouse and study gun-violence causes and prevention.

analysis.who_pays: Tens of millions of current handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners, who would need a federal license (with a fee of up to $10, plus application through a dealer) to keep guns they already own, face up to 10 years in prison for unlicensed possession, and must surrender guns within 48 hours if a license is denied or revoked. Licensed dealers would bear new record-keeping, verification, and inspection duties.
analysis.who_pays_short: Current handgun and rifle owners and gun dealers

drawbacks.text: Possessing a covered firearm without a license would carry up to 10 years in prison, so a gun owner who misses the compliance window for a gun bought before enactment faces felony exposure — the bill gave existing owners two years and new buyers one year.

A person whose license is denied or revoked must surrender the license and transfer out of their possession any covered firearm within 48 hours, with the burden later on the government at any appeal hearing — a swift consequence on a process run entirely by the Attorney General.

The bill strikes the existing statutory prohibition on establishing a firearms registration system and builds a federal record of sale containing serial numbers and owner information, even as another section states nothing in it should be construed to authorize a national registry — a tension gun-rights groups have long objected to in licensing-and-registry proposals.

Applicants must certify they were not a mental health facility patient in the prior five years and release their mental health records to the Attorney General, raising privacy and stigma concerns even for people who pose no danger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-safety logic is straightforward: licensing plus dealer-recorded sales makes it harder for prohibited people to get guns and easier to trace crime guns, and the fee is capped at $10 so cost is not the main barrier. The serious costs fall on law-abiding owners — a federal license requirement backed by felony penalties for possession, a 48-hour surrender rule, and a national transaction database — and the enforcement burden rests on the discretion of the Attorney General. Whether that trade is worth it is precisely the fight the bill never got to have: with zero cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, the merits were never weighed in public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its Crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the bill on May 11, 2022; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, where no further action was taken.
The bill had zero cosponsors, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 without any vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners and the firearms trade kept the existing rules — no federal licensing, no record of sale, no new possession penalties — because the bill never advanced. Communities affected by gun violence gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

for.name: Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, named for a Chicago student killed on a school bus in 2007, and the licensing-and-registry approach he had carried in earlier Congresses.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair with power to schedule markups and floor action (committee chaired by a Democrat in the 117th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Crime subcommittee on November 1, 2022 and never brought it to markup or the floor for the remaining months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so its level of support can only be measured by its sponsor — a Democrat — and its lack of any co-sponsorship.

industries.note: Every sale, transfer, and license application for covered firearms must run through a licensed dealer, making dealers the permanent paid gatekeepers of lawful gun ownership and charging owners a fee for the service.

Dealers must report the manufacturer, model, and serial number of every covered gun sold to the Attorney General, and the Attorney General collects production and sales figures; new licensing and transaction friction could reduce demand.

industries.industry: Current handgun and semiautomatic rifle owners
industries.note: Owners of guns bought before enactment had two years to obtain a federal license or face up to 10 years in prison, plus duties to report thefts, address changes, and to surrender guns after any denial or revocation.
